questions.stem: Which change in Earth's energy budget is described as the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: Extra aerosols from human activity reflect more incoming sunlight, so the surface warms further
Extra water vapour from human activity blocks incoming visible light, so the oceans store more heat
Extra greenhouse gases from human activity absorb more outgoing infrared, so less escapes to space
Extra ozone from human activity absorbs more incoming ultraviolet, so the lower atmosphere warms
questions.explanation: The enhanced greenhouse effect is the strengthening of the natural greenhouse effect as human activities raise greenhouse gas concentrations, so more outgoing infrared is absorbed and re-emitted and the surface warms. Aerosols mostly reflect sunlight and so tend to cool, not warm.

questions.stem: Fossil fuels contain no carbon-14 and are relatively low in carbon-13. Over the past century the proportions of both isotopes in atmospheric CO2 have fallen. What does this show?
options: Much of the added CO2 comes from volcanoes releasing carbon from the mantle
Much of the added CO2 comes from warming oceans releasing dissolved gas
Much of the added CO2 comes from the Sun producing more carbon-14 than before
Much of the added CO2 comes from burning ancient plant-derived carbon
questions.explanation: Carbon-14 decays away over tens of thousands of years, so carbon from fossil fuels millions of years old has none, and plant-derived carbon is low in carbon-13. Adding it dilutes both isotopes in the air. Volcanic and ocean carbon would not lower carbon-13 in this way.

questions.stem: Which human activity is the largest source of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide since the industrial revolution?
options: Applying nitrogen fertilisers
Using refrigerants in air-conditioners
Burning coal, oil and natural gas
Growing rice in flooded paddies
questions.explanation: Combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon stored for millions of years and is the largest source of the increase, with land clearing next. Rice paddies are a methane source and fertilisers a nitrous oxide source.

questions.stem: Which human activity is the main source of increased nitrous oxide in the atmosphere?
options: Generation of power from hydroelectric dams
Mining of iron ore in large open-cut pits
Release of refrigerants from old fridges
Use of nitrogen fertilisers in agriculture
questions.explanation: Soil microbes convert part of the nitrogen in fertilisers and manure into nitrous oxide, making agriculture the main human source. Refrigerants are sources of synthetic gases such as HFCs, not nitrous oxide.

questions.stem: Peat swamps store large amounts of partly decayed plant material. How does draining and burning peatland affect atmospheric greenhouse gases?
options: It has no effect because peat holds only nitrogen
It releases carbon stored over thousands of years as CO2
It removes CO2 because dry peat absorbs gas from the air
It adds oxygen that reacts with methane to form ozone
questions.explanation: Waterlogging slows decay, so peat builds up carbon over thousands of years. Draining lets oxygen in and decomposition speed up, and fire releases the carbon quickly as carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Fugitive emissions are a concern at coal mines and gas fields. What are they?
options: Planned releases of steam from cooling towers at power stations
Smoke from burning coal in homes, which contains black carbon
Dust blown from open-cut mines, which reflects sunlight to space
Unintended leaks of methane during extraction and transport
questions.explanation: Methane trapped in coal seams and gas reservoirs escapes during mining, drilling, processing and pipeline transport. Because methane has a high GWP, these leaks add significantly to emissions.

questions.stem: Why is the 1987 Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances often cited as a model for climate policy?
options: A local council scheme proved that taxes alone can change global air quality
A global agreement phased out a group of gases, and their levels then fell
A national law in one country solved a global problem without other nations
A voluntary industry code removed carbon dioxide from the air within a decade
questions.explanation: Nearly every nation agreed to phase out CFCs and related gases, and measurements show their atmospheric levels have since declined and the ozone layer is slowly recovering. It shows that coordinated global action can change atmospheric composition.

questions.stem: The Kigali Amendment, agreed in 2016, extended the Montreal Protocol to phase down which gases, and why?
options: Methane, because it is the main ozone-depleting gas
Carbon dioxide, because it destroys stratospheric ozone
HFCs, because many are powerful greenhouse gases
CFCs, because they had never yet been controlled
questions.explanation: HFCs replaced CFCs because they do not destroy ozone, but many have very high GWPs, so the Kigali Amendment phases them down to limit warming. CFCs were already controlled under the original protocol.

questions.stem: The Kyoto Protocol, adopted in 1997, was the first international agreement to:
options: set the same emission target for every nation
create the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
set binding emission targets for developed countries
ban the production of all chlorofluorocarbons
questions.explanation: Under the Kyoto Protocol developed countries accepted legally binding targets to cut greenhouse gas emissions, while developing countries had no binding targets. CFC phase-out came under the Montreal Protocol, and the IPCC was set up in 1988.

questions.stem: Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, how are national emission reductions decided?
options: Only developed countries set targets; others take no action
Each country must cut emissions by the same fixed percentage
Each country sets its own target, reviewed and raised over time
Each country is given a target by the United Nations each year
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement aims to hold warming well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels and to pursue 1.5 degrees. Each country sets its own nationally determined contribution, which is meant to become more ambitious in later rounds.

questions.stem: How does an emissions trading scheme aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions?
options: It charges a fee on imported goods according to the distance travelled
It caps total emissions and lets firms buy and sell permits to emit
It bans all fossil fuel use from a set date for every type of business
It pays every household a fixed amount to install rooftop solar panels
questions.explanation: A cap limits total emissions and permits are traded, so firms that can cut emissions cheaply do so and sell spare permits. The cap can be lowered over time. It does not ban fossil fuels outright.

questions.stem: A council plants street trees, installs solar panels on its buildings and switches to an electric vehicle fleet. A resident argues this is pointless because the town's emissions are tiny. Which response is best supported by the science?
options: Greenhouse gases stay near their source, so local cuts cool only the town
Greenhouse gases are removed within days, so local cuts act immediately
Greenhouse gases are produced only by industry, so councils cannot help
Greenhouse gases mix globally, so many local cuts together reduce warming
questions.explanation: Long-lived greenhouse gases mix through the whole atmosphere, so every tonne has the same effect wherever it is released. Global concentrations depend on the sum of many local, national and international actions, which is why policies at all three levels matter.

questions.stem: Which store holds the most carbon on Earth, exchanging it with the atmosphere only over millions of years?
options: Soils, as decaying organic material
Sedimentary rocks, such as limestone
Living vegetation on land and at sea
The atmosphere, as carbon dioxide gas
questions.explanation: Carbonate rocks and organic carbon in sediments hold far more carbon than the atmosphere, oceans, soils and living things combined. They exchange carbon only through slow processes such as weathering, burial and volcanic outgassing.

questions.stem: Which list orders carbon stores from shortest to longest typical storage time?
options: Deep ocean, atmosphere, living biomass, carbonate rock
Atmosphere, carbonate rock, living biomass, deep ocean
Atmosphere, living biomass, deep ocean, carbonate rock
Living biomass, atmosphere, carbonate rock, deep ocean
questions.explanation: Carbon cycles through the atmosphere in years, through living biomass in years to centuries, through the deep ocean over centuries to millennia, and stays in carbonate rock for millions of years. This is the difference between the fast and slow carbon cycles.

questions.stem: In the carbonate-silicate cycle, warmer, wetter conditions speed up chemical weathering of silicate rocks, which removes CO2. Why can this not offset present human emissions?
options: It stopped operating once land plants evolved and covered the rocks
It acts over hundreds of thousands of years, far slower than emissions
It adds CO2 to the air when it speeds up, so it increases the warming
It works only in polar regions, where there is too little rock exposed
questions.explanation: The carbonate-silicate cycle acts as Earth's long-term thermostat: warming increases weathering, drawing down carbon dioxide, which ends up in ocean carbonates. But it works over hundreds of thousands of years, so it cannot remove the carbon dioxide added within a few centuries.

questions.stem: In geosequestration, captured carbon dioxide is:
options: absorbed by fast-growing trees planted on land cleared for farming
frozen into blocks and stored in sealed tanks at the power station
compressed and injected into porous rock beneath an impermeable cap rock
dissolved in surface seawater, which carries it into the open ocean
questions.explanation: Geosequestration stores carbon dioxide deep underground, often in depleted gas fields or saline aquifers, where porous rock holds it and a cap rock above stops it rising. Tree planting is biological sequestration.

questions.stem: Which is the main geological risk to be managed in a geosequestration project?
options: Leakage of CO2 through faults or old wells
Melting of the reservoir rock by the CO2
Conversion of the CO2 into crude oil
Collapse of the cap rock into the mantle
questions.explanation: Stored carbon dioxide could escape upward along faults, fractures or poorly sealed old wells, so sites are chosen for a sound cap rock and monitored over the long term. Injected carbon dioxide does not melt rock or turn into oil.

questions.stem: The oceans currently absorb a large share of the CO2 that humans emit. Why might this sink become less effective as the climate warms?
options: Warmer water dissolves more CO2, so the oceans will soon become completely saturated
Warmer water releases more oxygen, which reacts with dissolved CO2 to make methane
Warmer water evaporates faster, so the oceans lose volume and hold less dissolved gas
Warmer water dissolves less CO2, and a more stratified ocean mixes it downward more slowly
questions.explanation: Gases are less soluble in warmer water, and warming strengthens layering of the upper ocean, slowing the transfer of carbon dioxide-rich surface water to depth. Both effects tend to weaken the ocean sink, a positive feedback.

questions.stem: Which statement about melting ice and sea level is correct?
options: Melting floating sea ice raises sea level; melting ice sheets on land barely does
Melting of any ice raises sea level by the same amount for the same mass of ice
Melting of ice lowers sea level, since water takes up less space than ice does
Melting ice sheets on land raise sea level; melting floating sea ice barely does
questions.explanation: Floating sea ice already displaces its own mass of seawater, so its melting adds very little to sea level. Ice sheets on Greenland and Antarctica sit on land, so meltwater flowing to the sea adds new water. Thermal expansion of warming seawater also raises sea level.

questions.stem: As the oceans absorb more CO2, which change threatens corals, molluscs and other shell-building organisms?
options: Lower pH and fewer carbonate ions for building shells
Higher pH and more calcium ions for building shells
Lower salinity and fewer nutrients for building shells
Higher oxygen and more nitrate for building shells
questions.explanation: Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which lowers ocean pH and reduces the carbonate ions that organisms need to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons. This is ocean acidification.

questions.stem: Why is thawing permafrost in high latitudes a concern for future climate?
options: Thawed ground absorbs methane from the air, ending its greenhouse effect
Thawed rock releases nitrogen, which forms a protective layer of ozone
Microbes decompose thawed organic matter, releasing CO2 and methane
Thawed soil reflects more sunlight, which cools the surrounding region
questions.explanation: Permafrost holds large amounts of frozen organic carbon. As it thaws, microbes break it down, releasing carbon dioxide where oxygen is present and methane in waterlogged soils, which amplifies warming. Thawing also causes ground to slump and damages infrastructure.

questions.stem: Methane clathrates (methane trapped in ice) occur in seafloor sediments on continental margins. They are stable only at high pressure and low temperature. What could happen if bottom waters warm?
options: Some clathrates could break down, releasing methane that adds to warming
The clathrates would grow larger, locking away more methane from the air
The clathrates would turn into coal, storing the carbon for millions of years
Some clathrates would release oxygen, which would raise seawater pH
questions.explanation: Warming bottom water can push clathrates outside their stability zone so they decompose and release methane. Some may be oxidised in the water to carbon dioxide, which adds to acidification, but any methane reaching the air is a potent greenhouse gas.

questions.stem: Field surveys show that many plant and animal species are now found further towards the poles and higher up mountains than in the past. Which explanation is best supported?
options: They are following ocean currents that have reversed direction
They are avoiding higher UV caused by the enhanced greenhouse effect
They are tracking suitable temperatures as the climate warms
They are escaping colder conditions caused by global cooling
questions.explanation: As regions warm, the temperatures a species tolerates move poleward and uphill, and species that can disperse follow them. Alpine species already at mountain tops have nowhere higher to go, which puts them at particular risk.

questions.stem: Hotter, drier conditions lengthen fire seasons in southern Australia. Which chain correctly links the spheres after a large bushfire?
options: Smoke cools the oceans, adding CO2; the cooler sea then causes more bushfires
Vegetation burns, releasing CO2 and smoke; bare soil then erodes into streams
Vegetation burns, absorbing CO2 and smoke; bare soil then holds more rainfall
Soil melts in the heat, releasing CO2; streams then carry the molten rock away
questions.explanation: Fire moves carbon from the biosphere to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide and smoke, and removes the plant cover that protects soil. Heavy rain on burnt slopes can then wash soil and ash into waterways, linking the geosphere and hydrosphere.

questions.stem: During a marine heatwave, corals on a reef turn white. What has happened?
options: The corals have been covered by white salt from evaporating seawater
The corals have been coated by sand stirred up by stronger currents
The corals have expelled the symbiotic algae living in their tissues
The corals have grown a new skeleton of white calcium carbonate
questions.explanation: Heat stress makes corals expel the symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) that give them colour and much of their food, exposing the white skeleton. If the heat lasts too long the corals may die.

questions.stem: Air sampled at the Kennaook/Cape Grim station in north-west Tasmania is valued as a baseline record of the Southern Hemisphere atmosphere. Why?
options: Its location near the equator gives air that is warmer than the global average
Westerly winds bring air that has crossed the Southern Ocean, far from pollution
Easterly winds bring air straight from mainland cities, showing urban pollution
Its height above the clouds means air there has never touched the surface
questions.explanation: Run jointly by the Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO since 1976, the station receives air from the west that has travelled thousands of kilometres over the Southern Ocean, so it represents well-mixed background air rather than local pollution.

questions.stem: A weather station's long temperature record shows a sudden 0.8 degree drop in one year, when the station was moved from a town centre to a nearby airport. What should scientists do with the record?
options: Adjust for the move, using nearby stations, so the record is consistent
Use the record unchanged, because any adjustment of data is dishonest
Treat the drop as real evidence of sudden regional climate cooling
Delete all data before the move, since the old site was too warm
questions.explanation: A sudden step at a known site change is a non-climatic error. Comparing with nearby stations lets scientists correct, or homogenise, the record so that real trends are not hidden or exaggerated. Treating the step as cooling would be a systematic error.

questions.stem: Surface weather stations, weather balloons, satellites and ocean floats all show global warming. Why does using several independent data sets increase confidence?
options: Agreement between different methods makes a shared error unlikely
More data sets always cancel out every random and systematic error
Each data set measures only one sphere, so each one is unreliable
Satellites alone give exact values, so the rest just add precision
questions.explanation: Each method has its own possible errors, so when methods that work in different ways agree, it is unlikely they share the same error. More data reduces random error but cannot by itself remove systematic error.

questions.stem: In climate science, a proxy is:
options: a computer model that predicts the climate of the future
an international agreement to report greenhouse gas data
indirect evidence of past climate preserved in natural materials
a direct thermometer reading taken at a weather station
questions.explanation: Proxies such as ice cores, tree rings, corals, pollen and microfossils record conditions indirectly. They extend climate records back far beyond the period of instrument measurements.

questions.stem: Ice sheets store water rich in the lighter oxygen-16 isotope. During a glacial period, how does the oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 ratio in the shells of deep-sea foraminifera change, and why?
options: It rises, because ice holds more oxygen-18 and the ocean water is warmer
It falls, because ice holds more oxygen-16 and the ocean water is colder
It rises, because ice holds more oxygen-16 and the ocean water is colder
It falls, because ice holds more oxygen-18 and the ocean water is warmer
questions.explanation: Water containing oxygen-16 evaporates more readily and becomes locked in ice sheets, leaving seawater enriched in oxygen-18; colder water also increases oxygen-18 uptake in shells. A higher ratio in foraminifera therefore indicates colder conditions and more ice.

questions.stem: Pollen grains in a lake's sediment layers change from rainforest species to grassland species upward through a core. What does this most likely record?
options: A change to a drier climate around the lake
A change to a wetter climate around the lake
A change in the lake's water to salt water
A change in the direction of the lake's inflow
questions.explanation: Pollen is preserved in layers and identifies the plants growing nearby, which reflect rainfall and temperature. A shift from rainforest to grassland pollen suggests the climate became drier.

questions.stem: A scientist wants yearly temperature estimates for the past 500 years in a temperate forest region, and another wants the climate of the past 400 000 years. Which proxies best suit each study?
options: Historical diaries for both, as they are most exact
Tree rings for the first, ice cores for the second
Ice cores for the first, tree rings for the second
Coral bands for the first, pollen for the second
questions.explanation: Tree rings give annual resolution but span only centuries to a few thousand years. Antarctic ice cores reach back hundreds of thousands of years, recording temperature through isotopes and carbon dioxide in trapped air. Diaries cover only recent centuries in some places.

questions.stem: Massive corals grow annual bands, and the chemistry of each band, such as its ratio of strontium to calcium, varies with water temperature. What can these corals provide?
options: A record of past glacier extent from scratches on the coral
A year-by-year record of past sea surface temperature
A record of past atmospheric CO2 trapped in air bubbles
A record of past rainfall on land from the widths of rings
questions.explanation: Coral growth bands can be counted like tree rings, and their chemistry records the temperature of the water in which they grew, giving yearly sea surface temperature records. Air bubbles are the source of carbon dioxide records in ice cores.

questions.stem: Scientists study the mid-Pliocene, about 3 million years ago, as an analogue for a future climate. Why is this period useful?
options: It was the coldest glacial period, so it shows the limits of natural climate change
It had no ice at the poles, so it shows climate with continents in very different places
CO2 was similar to levels now being approached, with continents near present positions
CO2 was far lower than now, so it shows what happens if emissions are reversed quickly
questions.explanation: In the mid-Pliocene, carbon dioxide was around 400 ppm, the continents and ocean gateways were close to their present arrangement, and the climate was warmer with higher sea levels. These similarities make it a useful, though imperfect, guide to a warmer future.

questions.stem: About 56 million years ago, at the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, a large release of carbon caused rapid warming and ocean acidification. Why is it an imperfect analogue for today?
options: Present emissions affect only the atmosphere, while that event affected oceans
Present carbon emissions are being released faster than the release at that time
That release was mainly oxygen, so it could not have caused the warming observed
Its warming was caused by a brighter Sun, so it tells us nothing about carbon
questions.explanation: The PETM shows how the Earth system responds to a large carbon release, including warming, acidification and species shifts. But estimates suggest carbon is now being released faster than during the PETM, which gives ecosystems and the slow carbon cycle less time to adjust.

questions.stem: How does a general circulation model (GCM) simulate climate?
options: It draws the best straight line through past temperatures and extends it
It uses only the latest satellite image to predict the next century of climate
It divides the atmosphere and oceans into a 3D grid and solves physical equations
It averages past weather records and repeats them unchanged into the future
questions.explanation: A GCM represents the atmosphere, oceans, land and ice as a three-dimensional grid of cells and calculates how energy, water and air move between them using the laws of physics. Extending a trend line cannot respond to new conditions such as different emissions.

questions.stem: Why do GCMs give more confident projections of global average temperature than of rainfall in one small catchment?
options: Small catchments have no weather, so there is nothing to predict
Their grid cells are large, so storms and clouds must be approximated
Rainfall is not included in any GCM, which models only temperature
Global temperature has never been measured, so it cannot be checked
questions.explanation: Grid cells are often tens to hundreds of kilometres across, so clouds, storms and local terrain smaller than a cell must be represented approximately. Global averages smooth out these local uncertainties.

questions.stem: Projections from several GCMs for 2100 cover a range of temperatures, and each model gives different results for different emissions scenarios. What is the best interpretation?
options: The range will disappear once one model is chosen as the correct one
The range reflects uncertainty in models and in future human choices
The range shows that GCMs are unreliable and should not be used at all
The range shows the warming will be the lowest value in every scenario
questions.explanation: Differences between models reflect uncertainty in processes such as clouds, while different scenarios reflect unknown future emissions. Using many models and scenarios shows the likely range of outcomes rather than one exact prediction.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)?
options: To assess published research on climate change and report to governments
To run its own weather stations and climate experiments around the world
To set and enforce legally binding emission targets for each nation
To fund new power stations that use renewable sources of energy
questions.explanation: Set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the United Nations Environment Programme, the IPCC brings together scientists worldwide to assess published research. Its reports inform negotiations, but targets are set by governments through agreements such as the Paris Agreement.
